Subject: RFI: Latency granularity & load matrix for inference endpoints

Hi Vanessa,

Thanks for the quick intro last week. As part of Helios' procurement RFI we'd like detailed, machine-actionable answers to the performance section so our SRE and procurement teams can validate vendor comparability. Specifically we need: 

- P50 / P95 / P99 latencies for token generation (ms) for sequence lengths: 32, 128, 512, 1024.
- Sustained throughput (tokens/sec and QPS) for 1, 5, 10, 20 concurrent connections under steady-state, for batch sizes: 1, 4, 8, 16.
- Cold start penalty (first request after idle) vs warm-run tail latency and how you measure it.
- Impact of KV cache reuse on latency for multi-turn chat flows (examples of cache hit vs miss).
- Behavior for quantized variants (8-bit/4-bit) vs FP16/F32 in terms of latency and quality tradeoffs.
- Test harness spec: workload generator (open-source tool or custom), traffic shaping, warmup heuristics, data sampling, and seed prompts.
- Any autoscaling / canary throttling behavior that affects observed throughput during burst scenarios.

Can you provide a populated latency/load matrix (spreadsheet) and a short description of your benchmark methodology? We prefer CSV/XLSX plus a short PDF summarizing assumptions. Also include links to the exact test harness we can run internally.

Target timeline: we’d like responses by Dec 20 so our SREs can baseline before year-end procurement meetings.

Thanks,
Priya Raman
Head of Platform Procurement
Helios Systems

Hi Priya —

Thanks for the clear ask. Attached is our initial latency/load matrix (redwood_latency_matrix_v1.xlsx) and a short PDF explaining the methodology. Highlights up front:

- We include P50/P95/P99 for seq lengths 32/128/512/1024 across three model classes (13B FP16, 33B FP16, 33B int8-4q).
- Throughput reported as tokens/sec and QPS measured at steady-state after a 120s warmup window; batch sizes 1/4/8/16; concurrency sweep 1–20.
- Cold start is captured by measuring the first request after a 15-minute idle; typical cold penalty is +12–45 ms depending on model and sequence length (details in spreadsheet).
- KV-cache hit vs miss: we include separate rows for continuous chat (cache hits on prefix) vs stateless prompts. Cache reuse reduces token-gen P99 by roughly 20–40% under identical concurrency.
- Quantized variants show 1.8–2.6x throughput improvement at the cost of a small quality delta (we include evaluation notes).

I’ve also attached a lightweight benchmark harness proposal (benchmark-harness-proposal.tar.gz) and included a pointer to our public harness repo. If it helps, we can run a mirrored test in our lab and invite your SREs to a live session.

Proposed next step: 30–45 minute calibration call so we can align sequences, sample prompts, and the exact success metric you'd prefer (e.g., 95th token latency vs end-to-end request completion). Are you available Dec 22 or Dec 28 for a canary run?

Best,

Vanessa / Marissa —

Reviewed the draft matrix. A few technical clarifications and proposed lab protocol below that you can paste into the Helios-facing PDF: 

Methodology (short):
- Hardware baseline: 4x NVIDIA A10G (FP16 paths) for the 13B and 33B FP16 runs; 8x A10G for sustained high-QPS 33B int8 runs to avoid PCIe/host bottlenecks.
- Models: redwood-13B.fp16, redwood-33B.fp16, redwood-33B.int8-q4 (quantized 4-bit).
- Sequence lengths: 32, 128, 512, 1024 token generation windows. For throughput we measure tokens/sec across a 5-minute steady-state window after warmup.
- Warmup: 120s synthetic traffic using the same distribution as test prompts; we recommend 120–300s for heavy quantized runs.
- Cold start: measure first end-to-end request after 15m idle for each variant; run the same request 5x spaced by 5s to compute mean/median and per-request deltas.
- KV cache: measure two modes — full-cache hit (100% prefix reuse) vs cold-cache (no reuse). Use a 10-step multi-turn chat scenario to compute per-token latency deltas.
- Batching: dynamic batching enabled with max batch size aligned to requested batch param (we emulate batch sizes 1/4/8/16 at the client level). Server-level batch coalescing will occasionally increase effective batch; we report both client-requested and observed effective batch sizes.

Representative numbers (lab, non-prod, 4xA10G):
- redwood-13B.fp16 @ seq=128, batch=1, concurrency=4: P50=12ms, P95=28ms, P99=45ms, throughput ~4200 tokens/sec.
- redwood-33B.fp16 @ seq=512, batch=4, concurrency=8: P50=48ms, P95=120ms, P99=210ms, throughput ~5200 tokens/sec.
- redwood-33B.int8-q4 @ seq=512, batch=8, concurrency=10: P50=22ms, P95=60ms, P99=110ms, throughput ~11000 tokens/sec.

Caveats and notes for Helios:
- Quantized throughput numbers assume the model was converted with our vetted post-training quantization pipeline; quality regression checks are included in the attached PDF.
- Observed tail latency is strongly correlated with tokenization variance and bursty concurrent small requests; we recommend request coalescing for high-percentile stability.
- For longer sequences (1024) memory-bound behavior can appear and will be reflected as higher P99s; in those cases we recommend stepping down concurrency or moving to a larger GPU pool.

Test harness: see https://github.com/redwood-inference/bench-harness/tree/helios-proposal — it includes workload generator (gload), sample prompt sets, and a reproducible infra-as-code plan (k8s job & terraform snippet) to run a mirrored test.

If you want, I can prepare a shorter one-page cheat sheet for Helios SREs summarizing the exact commands to run.

—Aditya
